en: Let the tumult split the sky!
Let the earth crack and part,
Let the doomed shed their blood,
Let dust fly up to heaven,
Scatter his blood like water.
Mighty Kyrgyz, you are our wings;
To strike down a charging foe
Is the custom left by your forefathers.
From time beyond remembering,
When has this strife ever ceased?
Since the earth was made and peoples arose,
Since our tribe became Kyrgyz,
There has been no reckoning of the dead.
We suffered humiliation and gathered again;
Harried and scattered by the enemy,
We were oppressed for seven generations.
First we were in Altai,
Many were scattered to Kanghai,
Many of us went away to Eren,
For our persecuting enemies were many;
Many Kyrgyz descended
Into depths from which none returned.
Because of cruel enemies,
At times we scattered,
Beyond the land of El-Körbös;
At times we Kyrgyz went
Among the people of Hindustan.
Blood was shed in combat;
From age to age,
From time to time,
We Kyrgyz suffered mighty oppression
And were divided by the measure of the lash.
Despite enemies who dealt us wrath,
Our precious lives still appeared alive.
When hostile enemies came,
We clashed and battled;
Blood was shed and warriors died,
But the formidable, blessed Kyrgyz people
Never failed to take revenge,
For honor and for the people.
Their heroes died.”
So spoke the brave gray wolf,
The princely son of Manas,
Stirring a great commotion throughout the world.
He makes us slaves lower than beasts.
He lets us sow no crops,
He lets us camp nowhere freely,
He lets us tether not even two mares.
He will unleash his wrath upon the multitude,
Reduce this land to less than a hair,
And mercilessly slaughter these people.
With brave Seytek and Külchoro
Proclaimed the leaders of the people,
What inheritance shall we gain?
Let us spare not a single life
And perish fighting;
O wretched Kyrgyz people,
Let us pass away as sacrifices.
When the khan dies, let the people die;
Let the whole multitude die!
Once the head that leads is gone,
Once you die and your days are done,
Let the eyes of this fallen head close in peace,
So that the multitude left behind
May see days of happiness!
The wrathful Sarybai
Is a flood that will engulf us,
A black and blazing fire,
A deadly bullet from a matchlock;
His breath burns the soul,
He is an ember huge as Mount Kap.
O lion-born descendants of the Kyrgyz,
Turn aside in every direction
The raging flood he drives upon us!
Stand tall and bare your breasts
Before death’s bullets;
O dear people, vast as lake and river,
Summon the strength to quench
His red embers, huge as Mount Kap.
Advance and extinguish the fire;
That swine who seeks to rule,
Bind him by a hair
And cast him down.
Do not make Sarybai a giant,
Let us bind him by a hair and cast him down.
Do not make Sarybai a giant,
Do not let him rule this Talas;
Let our blood flow like water,
Let us all perish!
Rather than be ambushed from the heights,
And have every valiant lion
Delivered into Sarybai’s hands,
Rather than lose mane and tail
And wander stripped and forlorn,
Rather than live with broken horns,
Polled and powerless,
Calling Sarybai our lord,
And burning in anguish,
Let us flee Talas in terror,
And, fighting seven years without cease,
Ransack every last saddlebag
Of the infidel monster’s son.
Let the multitude begin the battle;
Old men bent low and growing youths alike,
Let us abandon everything,
And rise in open strife
Against the oppressor.
Without delay, level your spears;
Let us wage a furious battle.
Brave Semetey, Külchoro,
And brave Seytek, whom we make our hope—
Let the whole people take these three
As the girdle around their waists.
Against the tyrant’s forces,
Let us stand in bitter battle.
If Sarybai is truly a hero,
Let us perish in slaughter.
The people surge like a river;
When the river floods and torrents run,
We shall see what Sarybai is worth—
Let us grapple with that dog!”
The people cried out in tumult,
In a roar that split the heavens;
Horns and trumpets sounded,
Warriors spoke and the people grew impassioned,
Voicing countless words.
Brave young men and thoroughbred steeds,
All together grew impassioned.
Wisdom took the lead;
Not only their livestock but their lives
The multitude renounced, saying,
“The hero’s words are true.”
“How can anyone say we shall not face
Cannon fire and turmoil?
If hostile death has reached us,
If it is written upon our necks, let us see it;
Let us stand as support
For the hero, pillar of our inheritance!
Sarybai is your true enemy;
Let us truly beat out his madness.”
The people cried these words aloud:
“Your words are true, hero;
What you propose is wise.
Let us all depart from Sarybai,
That godless infidel.
If we hold back, may the cliffs strike us,
May the towering Ala-Too strike us!
Your words are not in vain,
My noble-born sultan;
You have found us sound counsel.
If we spare ourselves from Sarybai,
May the matchlock’s flame strike us,
May the musket’s bullet strike us,
May the broad-breasted earth strike us,
May the whole vault of heaven strike us!
Rather than live as captive slaves,
Fallen into Sarybai’s hands,
Clad in black mourning,
Burning until we become embers,
Crushed and brought to nothing,
Rather than see our children torn away
And lie enduring humiliation,
Let us begin the true slaughter,
And make our poor souls shriek,
The Kyrgyz pondered and rose in turmoil;
The mighty kinsman, the valiant lion,
Donned his armor impervious to bullets,
Separated himself from the people and rode out alone.
Behold such a gray-wolf warrior,
Appearing like a lofty blue crag;
Before him he was a grim tiger—
When he set his will, no living soul could match him,
And no foe who faced him prospered.
Behold such a gray-wolf warrior,
Appearing like a hill
Upon a boundless plain,
Like a link in the chain of true steel
That encircled
The entire world.
He appeared like the fruit
Of the tree of life
That nourishes the world.
He went to confront Sarybai,
To meet him face-to-face,
To die if hostile death had come;
At all times he was the people’s wing,
A fortress before the nation—
It was his custom to ride out in single combat.
Whoever beheld him lost all composure;
He appeared to be the pillar
Supporting the one created world,
The roost
Of the giant black zymyr bird.
When he charged, his wrath poured forth;
Such was the bloodthirsty warrior,
Appearing like a towering mountain.
His spirit was lofty, his venom strong,
And he leveled all who attacked him.
“We are dead if we behold that butcher—
Abandon hope for your precious lives!”
Terrifying all who saw him,
He made his splendid thoroughbred
Amble proudly,
And, heading straight for Sarybai,
Prepared to enter the massed host
And attack him.
Countless broad-bladed spears
Loamed huge as they rose from men’s hands,
And steel-hafted battle-axes
Appeared in the people’s grasp.
All the warriors surged with fervor,
While the fainthearted, rash in courage,
Panted without leading the people;
The champions spread out to the flanks,
And cowards who dared not leave their doors
Were trapped in the very midst,
Wondering what would happen now.
All was torn into confusion,
And thus appeared before the countless host;
As the people mounted and stood ready,
Then Semetey
Prepared himself like a hawk,
And inspiration from the unseen
Came to the precious lion.
His departure from this world,
His confronting his enemy Sarybai,
And meeting him face-to-face had come.
He was eager to devour whoever crossed him;
His two eyes became four.
For the people, the precious lion
Was ready to sacrifice himself.
Behold, such was the conflict,
Such was the chaos that descended;
Though the broad world had not narrowed,
The cunning Sarybai
Had embroiled the whole universe in strife.
He himself seemed corruption incarnate;
Against the black eye of disaster,
Against the very taker of souls,
The great lion, son of Manas,
The steadfast, ill-fated hero,
Set all his weapons in order,
Strapped on his gleaming sword,
And took up his steel-hafted spear.
When he came over the rise
And saw Sarybai’s form—
If you looked upon Sarybai,
He was like a lion clawing the earth;
At the infidel’s very silhouette,
Every mortal human being
Fled far away, daring not approach.
His brow and head sagged heavily;
The wrathful infidel’s brow
Stretched like a vast wasteland,
As though his gaze would swallow a soul.
He carried a whip like a pine tree,
